questions.stem: In these paired coronary angiograms, panel A (arrow) shows an abrupt occlusion of a coronary artery and panel B shows the same vessel with restored flow. What procedure produced the change from A to B?

explanation.summary: The occluded segment in A is reopened in B by percutaneous coronary intervention, in which a catheter-delivered balloon and stent restore antegrade flow, the definitive reperfusion strategy for STEMI.
explanation.whyCorrect: The occluded segment in A is reopened in B by percutaneous coronary intervention, in which a catheter-delivered balloon and stent restore antegrade flow, the definitive reperfusion strategy for STEMI.

questions.stem: This figure contrasts NSTEMI (partially occlusive thrombus) with STEMI (completely occlusive thrombus). The complete coronary occlusion of STEMI characteristically produces which pattern of myocardial injury?

explanation.summary: A completely occlusive thrombus halts flow to the full thickness of the myocardium supplied, producing transmural infarction and ST-segment elevation, whereas a partially occlusive thrombus in NSTEMI typically causes subendocardial injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: A completely occlusive thrombus halts flow to the full thickness of the myocardium supplied, producing transmural infarction and ST-segment elevation, whereas a partially occlusive thrombus in NSTEMI typically causes subendocardial injury.

questions.stem: This coagulation cascade highlights the sites where heparin acts (factor Xa and thrombin/IIa). By what molecular mechanism does heparin inhibit these factors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It directly binds thrombin's active site without a cofactor

choices.label: B
choices.text: It inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase

choices.label: D
choices.text: It potentiates antithrombin III, which then inactivates the factors

explanation.summary: Heparin binds antithrombin III and dramatically accelerates its inactivation of thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa; it therefore requires adequate antithrombin III to be effective and works indirectly rather than by direct enzyme inhibition.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heparin binds antithrombin III and dramatically accelerates its inactivation of thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa; it therefore requires adequate antithrombin III to be effective and works indirectly rather than by direct enzyme inhibition.

questions.stem: This diagram shows aspirin blocking platelet cyclooxygenase (COX) to prevent thromboxane A2 synthesis. Because aspirin's inhibition of platelet COX is irreversible, how long does its antiplatelet effect persist after a single dose?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only a few hours until it is metabolized

choices.label: E
choices.text: For the lifespan of the affected platelets

explanation.summary: Platelets lack nuclei and cannot synthesize new cyclooxygenase, so aspirin's irreversible COX inhibition lasts the ~7-10 day lifespan of the exposed platelets until new platelets are produced.
explanation.whyCorrect: Platelets lack nuclei and cannot synthesize new cyclooxygenase, so aspirin's irreversible COX inhibition lasts the ~7-10 day lifespan of the exposed platelets until new platelets are produced.

questions.stem: This diagram shows tPA converting plasminogen to plasmin, which degrades fibrin into fragments. Which laboratory test measures these fibrin degradation products clinically?

explanation.summary: Plasmin cleaves cross-linked fibrin into degradation products, the most specific of which is D-dimer; an elevated D-dimer reflects active clot breakdown and is used in the workup of venous thromboembolism.
explanation.whyCorrect: Plasmin cleaves cross-linked fibrin into degradation products, the most specific of which is D-dimer; an elevated D-dimer reflects active clot breakdown and is used in the workup of venous thromboembolism.

questions.stem: This diagram shows a fibrin-rich thrombus being broken down, with the circled laboratory marker rising. What does elevation of that marker reflect?

explanation.summary: The circled marker is released when plasmin degrades cross-linked fibrin within a clot; its elevation is a sensitive but nonspecific indicator of active clot formation and breakdown, useful for excluding DVT when low.
explanation.whyCorrect: The circled marker is released when plasmin degrades cross-linked fibrin within a clot; its elevation is a sensitive but nonspecific indicator of active clot formation and breakdown, useful for excluding DVT when low.

questions.stem: This paired imaging test evaluates whether a vein flattens under probe pressure to detect thrombus. What imaging modality is this?

explanation.summary: In compression ultrasound, a normal vein collapses fully under probe pressure; a vein that fails to compress contains thrombus. It is the first-line imaging test for diagnosing deep vein thrombosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In compression ultrasound, a normal vein collapses fully under probe pressure; a vein that fails to compress contains thrombus. It is the first-line imaging test for diagnosing deep vein thrombosis.

questions.stem: This flowchart integrates pretest probability (Wells score), D-dimer testing, and compression ultrasound. Which clinical decision does it support?

explanation.summary: The algorithm combines clinical pretest probability, D-dimer, and compression ultrasound results to confirm or rule out DVT while minimizing unnecessary imaging.
explanation.whyCorrect: The algorithm combines clinical pretest probability, D-dimer, and compression ultrasound results to confirm or rule out DVT while minimizing unnecessary imaging.

questions.stem: This patient has unilateral swelling, erythema, and dusky discoloration of the left lower limb. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Acute unilateral leg swelling with discoloration and warmth reflects venous outflow obstruction from a deep vein thrombosis; the contrast with the normal opposite limb supports a localized venous cause.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute unilateral leg swelling with discoloration and warmth reflects venous outflow obstruction from a deep vein thrombosis; the contrast with the normal opposite limb supports a localized venous cause.

questions.stem: The diagram shows a clot fixed within a vein and, below, a fragment of that clot breaking free and moving downstream. What is the most dangerous consequence when such a fragment travels through the venous circulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It dissolves harmlessly before reaching any organ

choices.label: B
choices.text: It settles in the coronary arteries, causing myocardial infarction

choices.label: C
choices.text: It travels to the brain, causing an ischemic stroke

choices.label: D
choices.text: It lodges in the pulmonary arteries, causing pulmonary embolism

choices.label: E
choices.text: It blocks the renal artery, causing acute kidney injury

explanation.summary: A detached venous thrombus (embolus) follows venous return to the right heart and is pumped into the pulmonary arteries, where it obstructs pulmonary blood flow, i.e., a pulmonary embolism. Venous emboli reach the lungs, not the systemic arterial circulation, unless a right-to-left shunt exists.
explanation.whyCorrect: A detached venous thrombus (embolus) follows venous return to the right heart and is pumped into the pulmonary arteries, where it obstructs pulmonary blood flow, i.e., a pulmonary embolism. Venous emboli reach the lungs, not the systemic arterial circulation, unless a right-to-left shunt exists.

questions.stem: This figure links a clot at a lower-leg deep vein (bottom) with a blockage in the lungs (top) by way of the large central vein. What pathophysiologic sequence does it illustrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An arterial plaque ruptures and travels to the legs

choices.label: B
choices.text: A lower-limb thrombus embolizes up the IVC into the lungs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bronchial mucus plugs migrate into the pulmonary veins

choices.label: D
choices.text: A leg infection spreads through lymphatics to the lung

choices.label: E
choices.text: A lung clot showers emboli down into the leg veins

explanation.summary: A deep vein thrombosis in the leg can dislodge and travel up the inferior vena cava to the right heart, then into the pulmonary arteries, producing a pulmonary embolism. This DVT-to-PE progression is the central danger of lower-extremity venous thrombosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A deep vein thrombosis in the leg can dislodge and travel up the inferior vena cava to the right heart, then into the pulmonary arteries, producing a pulmonary embolism. This DVT-to-PE progression is the central danger of lower-extremity venous thrombosis.

questions.stem: This clinical photograph (arrow) shows one calf that is noticeably larger and more swollen than the other. In a patient with recent immobilization, this asymmetric finding most strongly suggests which diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Unilateral leg swelling, with one calf larger than the other, is a classic sign of deep vein thrombosis. The obstructing venous thrombus impairs outflow, causing edema, warmth, and tenderness confined to that limb, unlike the symmetric swelling of systemic causes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unilateral leg swelling, with one calf larger than the other, is a classic sign of deep vein thrombosis. The obstructing venous thrombus impairs outflow, causing edema, warmth, and tenderness confined to that limb, unlike the symmetric swelling of systemic causes.

questions.stem: This Venn diagram places thrombosis at the intersection of endothelial damage, a hypercoagulable state, and abnormal blood flow/venous stasis. By what eponymous name is this trio of predisposing factors known?

explanation.summary: The three overlapping contributors to thrombus formation, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability, and stasis/turbulent flow, constitute Virchow's triad. Any one component predisposes to thrombosis, and their overlap markedly increases risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: The three overlapping contributors to thrombus formation, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability, and stasis/turbulent flow, constitute Virchow's triad. Any one component predisposes to thrombosis, and their overlap markedly increases risk.

questions.stem: A hospitalized, immobile patient has these inflatable sleeves wrapped around the calves and thighs, cyclically inflating and deflating. What is the primary purpose of this device?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Immobilize a fractured tibia during healing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Promote venous return and prevent deep vein thrombosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduce arterial blood pressure in the lower limb

choices.label: D
choices.text: Warm the extremity to treat hypothermia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deliver localized chemotherapy to the leg

explanation.summary: This is an intermittent pneumatic compression device. By rhythmically compressing the legs it augments venous flow and counteracts the venous stasis of Virchow's triad, providing mechanical prophylaxis against DVT in immobile patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is an intermittent pneumatic compression device. By rhythmically compressing the legs it augments venous flow and counteracts the venous stasis of Virchow's triad, providing mechanical prophylaxis against DVT in immobile patients.

questions.stem: The upper vessel shows blood moving in smooth parallel streamlines while the lower vessel shows chaotic swirling eddies. Which flow pattern (and associated hemodynamic condition) most favors venous thrombus formation?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only high-velocity laminar flow promotes clotting

explanation.summary: Laminar flow (top) keeps cells centered and endothelium undisturbed, whereas turbulence and stasis (bottom) allow platelet contact with the wall, activate clotting factors, and injure endothelium, the flow abnormalities of Virchow's triad that promote thrombosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Laminar flow (top) keeps cells centered and endothelium undisturbed, whereas turbulence and stasis (bottom) allow platelet contact with the wall, activate clotting factors, and injure endothelium, the flow abnormalities of Virchow's triad that promote thrombosis.

questions.stem: The boxed drugs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) block the circled clotting factor in this cascade. That factor normally catalyzes which reaction?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cross-linking of fibrin by factor XIII

choices.label: D
choices.text: Activation of factor VII by tissue factor

explanation.summary: Factor Xa sits at the start of the common pathway and converts prothrombin (II) to thrombin (IIa); the '-xaban' direct oral anticoagulants inhibit Xa, reducing thrombin generation and clot formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Factor Xa sits at the start of the common pathway and converts prothrombin (II) to thrombin (IIa); the '-xaban' direct oral anticoagulants inhibit Xa, reducing thrombin generation and clot formation.

questions.stem: An indwelling catheter in a hand vein produces localized redness, and the adjacent vein contains a clot with wall inflammation. This combination is best described as which condition?

explanation.summary: Trauma from an indwelling catheter injures the venous endothelium, promoting inflammation and clot formation within a superficial vein, i.e., superficial thrombophlebitis, typically presenting as a tender, red, cord-like vessel.
explanation.whyCorrect: Trauma from an indwelling catheter injures the venous endothelium, promoting inflammation and clot formation within a superficial vein, i.e., superficial thrombophlebitis, typically presenting as a tender, red, cord-like vessel.

questions.stem: This three-circle diagram shows the central overlap of endothelial damage, a hypercoagulable state, and abnormal blood flow. The central intersection represents the outcome favored when all three coexist. Clinically, which scenario most directly reflects this concept?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Postoperative immobility plus a vessel injury and inherited clotting tendency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hemolysis from a mechanical valve alone

explanation.summary: The figure depicts Virchow triad: endothelial injury, hypercoagulability, and stasis (abnormal flow). Convergence of these factors, as in an immobile postoperative patient with vessel injury and a thrombophilia, predisposes to venous thrombosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The figure depicts Virchow triad: endothelial injury, hypercoagulability, and stasis (abnormal flow). Convergence of these factors, as in an immobile postoperative patient with vessel injury and a thrombophilia, predisposes to venous thrombosis.

questions.stem: This leg shows a tender, erythematous, indurated cord-like streak with reddish nodularity tracking along the course of a superficial vein. This finding is most consistent with which diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A palpable, tender, red cord following a superficial vein reflects thrombosis with surrounding inflammation of that vein (superficial thrombophlebitis), distinct from the diffuse swelling of DVT or the septal panniculitis of erythema nodosum.
explanation.whyCorrect: A palpable, tender, red cord following a superficial vein reflects thrombosis with surrounding inflammation of that vein (superficial thrombophlebitis), distinct from the diffuse swelling of DVT or the septal panniculitis of erythema nodosum.

questions.stem: A patient's lower legs are shown: one leg has marked distal swelling, skin thickening, and dark discoloration compared with the other. What chronic condition does this appearance most likely represent?

explanation.summary: Long-standing venous hypertension from valvular incompetence produces dependent edema, skin thickening, and hemosiderin/pigment changes of the lower leg, the hallmark of chronic venous insufficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Long-standing venous hypertension from valvular incompetence produces dependent edema, skin thickening, and hemosiderin/pigment changes of the lower leg, the hallmark of chronic venous insufficiency.

questions.stem: The medial ankle and foot show brownish pigmentation, induration, and scaling in a patient with long-standing venous disease. This skin change is best described as?

explanation.summary: Chronic venous hypertension causes red-cell extravasation; breakdown of hemoglobin deposits hemosiderin, giving the characteristic brown pigmentation and eczematous change of stasis dermatitis in the gaiter area.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic venous hypertension causes red-cell extravasation; breakdown of hemoglobin deposits hemosiderin, giving the characteristic brown pigmentation and eczematous change of stasis dermatitis in the gaiter area.

questions.stem: A dilated, tortuous, rope-like subcutaneous vein bulges from the calf of this patient. What is this finding?

explanation.summary: Sustained venous reflux dilates superficial veins into the visible, tortuous, elongated cords known as varicose veins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sustained venous reflux dilates superficial veins into the visible, tortuous, elongated cords known as varicose veins.

questions.stem: Both lower legs show woody induration with confluent purple-brown discoloration and scaling over the gaiter region in advanced venous disease. This end-stage skin/subcutaneous change is termed?

explanation.summary: Chronic venous hypertension drives fibrosis of dermis and subcutaneous fat, producing the firm, hyperpigmented, inverted-champagne-bottle change called lipodermatosclerosis, often preceding venous ulceration.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic venous hypertension drives fibrosis of dermis and subcutaneous fat, producing the firm, hyperpigmented, inverted-champagne-bottle change called lipodermatosclerosis, often preceding venous ulceration.

questions.stem: This diagram contrasts normal and abnormal venous return in the leg. What underlying defect explains the abnormal (refluxing) blood flow and varicosities shown on the right?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Occlusion of the deep vein by thrombus

explanation.summary: When one-way venous valves fail, blood refluxes distally under gravity, raising venous pressure and dilating superficial veins into varicosities, in contrast with competent valves that direct flow upward.
explanation.whyCorrect: When one-way venous valves fail, blood refluxes distally under gravity, raising venous pressure and dilating superficial veins into varicosities, in contrast with competent valves that direct flow upward.

questions.stem: The illustration shows a needle injecting an agent directly into a superficial vein, with a magnified view of the vein lumen filling with a fibrotic/occluding mass. What treatment does this depict?

explanation.summary: Sclerotherapy injects a chemical sclerosant into the target vein, damaging the endothelium so the vein fibroses and is obliterated, as shown by the occluded lumen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sclerotherapy injects a chemical sclerosant into the target vein, damaging the endothelium so the vein fibroses and is obliterated, as shown by the occluded lumen.

questions.stem: This 4-step sequence shows a catheter introduced and advanced up a vein, then the vein narrowing and closing as the catheter is withdrawn. By what mechanism is the vein closed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The vein is surgically tied off and removed

choices.label: B
choices.text: A metal stent holds the vein permanently open

choices.label: C
choices.text: Thermal energy from the catheter injures the vein wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: A chemical sclerosant is injected into the lumen

choices.label: E
choices.text: A clot-dissolving drug is infused to reopen it

explanation.summary: Endovenous thermal (radiofrequency or laser) ablation delivers heat that denatures the vein wall collagen, causing contraction and fibrotic closure as the catheter is slowly withdrawn.
explanation.whyCorrect: Endovenous thermal (radiofrequency or laser) ablation delivers heat that denatures the vein wall collagen, causing contraction and fibrotic closure as the catheter is slowly withdrawn.
